note:
Geriatrics specialty clinic dictation. This is an 85-year-old male seen today for frailty and unintentional weight loss. He lives with his daughter, who tells me he has lost about 12 pounds over the past four months without trying. He reports poor appetite and feeling weak and tired, and says food just does not taste good anymore. He has hypertension, well controlled on amlodipine 5 mg daily, and takes no other regular medications. He denies vomiting, denies diarrhea, no abdominal pain, no difficulty swallowing, and no blood in the stool. He also denies cough, fever, and night sweats. Depression screening was negative today.

Vital signs, blood pressure 128/74, heart rate 72, temperature 98.2 F, weight 138 pounds, which is down from 150 pounds in the clinic record. On exam he appears thin and frail, mucous membranes are moist, heart regular, lungs clear, abdomen soft and nontender without masses. He needed his arms to rise from the chair and his gait is slow, about 0.6 meters per second.

Impression is frailty with unintentional weight loss, likely multifactorial with poor appetite as the main driver, and no alarm features on history. Plan, I will order a CBC, a comprehensive metabolic panel, a TSH, an albumin level, and a chest x-ray. Start an oral nutrition supplement twice daily between meals. Refer to the dietitian and to physical therapy for strength training. I asked the daughter to keep a food diary. Return to clinic in four weeks to repeat his weight and review the results.
summary: An 85-year-old male was seen in a geriatrics specialty clinic for frailty and unintentional weight loss of about 12 pounds over four months, with poor appetite, weakness, and tiredness. He has hypertension controlled on amlodipine and denied vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, difficulty swallowing, blood in the stool, cough, fever, and night sweats; depression screening was negative. He appeared thin and frail with a slow gait, and his weight was 138 pounds, down from 150. The impression was frailty with unintentional weight loss, likely multifactorial, without alarm features. Plan includes laboratory tests, a chest x-ray, an oral nutrition supplement, dietitian and physical therapy referrals, and a return visit in four weeks.

note:
25-year-old male, rheum clinic, f/u widespread MSK pain x ~14 mo, referred by PCP.

CC: diffuse aching pain, neck/shoulders/low back worst, w/ fatigue + poor sleep.
HPI: pain 6/10 daily, worse w/ stress + poor sleep, better w/ warm showers + light walking. Wakes unrefreshed, up 2-3x/night. Brain fog. Tension-type HA ~2x/wk, resolves w/ rest. No joint swelling, no morning stiffness >30 min, no rash, no fever, no wt loss, no oral ulcers, no eye redness. Denies depressed mood, denies SI. No hx trauma or recent infxn.
PMH: none sig. FH neg for autoimmune dz. Social: grad student, caffeine 3 cups/d, no tobacco, no EtOH.
Meds: duloxetine 30 mg daily x 4 wk (started by PCP), minimal benefit. Naproxen 500 mg BID x 3 mo, no help. Acetaminophen 500 mg PRN.

VS: BP 118/72, HR 68, Temp 98.4 F, wt 74 kg.
Exam: NAD, mood/affect nl. Diffusely tender over trapezius, lateral epicondyles, gluteal, medial knee fat pads. No synovitis hands/wrists/knees/ankles. FROM all joints, strength 5/5, DTR 2+ sym, gait nl. Skin: no rash, no psoriasis. Widespread pain index 12, SSS 8.
Labs (last wk): CBC nl (WBC 6.4, Hgb 15.1), ESR 5, CRP <0.3 mg/dL, TSH 2.1, CK nl, ANA neg, 25-OH vit D 31.

Impression: fibromyalgia (WPI 12 + SSS 8, sx >3 mo), labs neg for inflammatory dz. Non-restorative sleep contributing. Tension-type HA.
Tx: incr duloxetine to 60 mg daily. Start cyclobenzaprine 5 mg qHS. D/c naproxen (no benefit). Cont acetaminophen 500 mg PRN. Educated re dx + benign course, sleep hygiene, graded aerobic exercise (start 10 min walks, build to 30 min 3-5x/wk). Referral to PT and CBT. F/u 8 wk, sooner if new joint swelling, fever, wt loss.

He denied joint swelling, prolonged morning stiffness, rash, fever, weight loss, oral ulcers, eye redness, and depressed mood. Exam showed diffuse tenderness without synovitis, and CBC, ESR, CRP, TSH, CK, and ANA were unremarkable. The impression was fibromyalgia with contributing non-restorative sleep. Duloxetine was increased to 60 mg daily, cyclobenzaprine 5 mg at bedtime was started, naproxen was stopped, and PT and CBT referrals were made with follow-up in 8 weeks.

note:
Telehealth video visit, synchronous video with the patient's mother present and participating. The patient is a 4-year-old female seen for hard stools for about three months.

History per mother: she passes a hard, pellet-like stool every three to four days, with straining and crying, and sometimes holds it in and hides when she needs to go. She has occasional mild lower abdominal discomfort that resolves after she stools. Appetite is good. Mother denies blood in the stool, vomiting, fever, weight loss, and diarrhea. Diet is low in fiber with few fruits and vegetables and about three cups of cow's milk a day. She has been toilet trained for urine since age three. No chronic medical conditions and no regular medications. Extra water has helped little.

Home measurements reported by mother: temperature 98.2 F, weight 16.5 kg on the home scale.

Limited video exam: she is playful, active, well-appearing, and in no distress, with comfortable breathing. Mother pressed on her abdomen under guidance and the child did not wince or show tenderness; the abdomen did not look distended. A rectal exam is not possible by video.

Impression is functional constipation without alarm features. Plan: start polyethylene glycol 3350, 8.5 g (half a capful) mixed in 4 ounces of juice once daily, adjusting to one soft stool each day. Limit milk to two cups a day and add fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. Scheduled toilet sitting for five minutes after meals with a footstool, and a sticker chart for stooling. Call or return for blood in the stool, repeated vomiting, fever, or worsening abdominal pain. Follow-up video visit in three weeks.

Mother denied blood in the stool, vomiting, fever, weight loss, and diarrhea, and the limited video exam showed a well-appearing child without abdominal tenderness or distension. The impression was functional constipation without alarm features. Polyethylene glycol 3350 daily was started with dietary changes, scheduled toilet sitting, return precautions, and a video follow-up in three weeks.

note:
Hospital day 3 for this 96-year-old female admitted with two weeks of worsening urinary incontinence and new confusion. Overnight she had no falls and no fever. She slept well, and her confusion is better this morning; she is oriented to person and place. The nurse documents four episodes of incontinence in the past 24 hours, mostly with urgency when she cannot reach the toilet in time. She denies dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, and abdominal pain.

Her history includes atrial fibrillation on apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily, hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily, and chronic constipation. Oxybutynin 5 mg three times daily was started by her outpatient provider three weeks ago for bladder urgency, and it is likely contributing to her confusion and constipation.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 98.1 F, blood pressure 132/70, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. She is thin, alert, and cooperative. Heart rhythm is irregularly irregular without a murmur, lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft with mild lower abdominal fullness but no suprapubic tenderness. There is no costovertebral angle tenderness, and the perineal skin is intact. Admission urinalysis showed trace leukocyte esterase and negative nitrite, and the urine culture finalized with no growth. Bladder scan post-void residual was 45 mL. Basic metabolic panel: sodium 138, potassium 4.1, creatinine 1.0. Hemoglobin 11.8.

My impression is urge urinary incontinence worsened by oxybutynin, which is also a likely contributor to her confusion, along with chronic constipation. There is no urinary tract infection, so no antibiotics are needed. Her atrial fibrillation remains anticoagulated.

Plan: stop oxybutynin today. Start timed voiding every two hours while awake with a bedside commode and nurse assistance. Start polyethylene glycol 17 g daily for constipation. Continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Avoid an indwelling urinary catheter because of the risk of infection and hematuria while she is anticoagulated. Request PT and OT evaluation. Repeat basic metabolic panel tomorrow. Anticipate discharge in one to two days with geriatrics clinic follow-up in two weeks.

note:
This 52-year-old male was seen in the infectious disease clinic for fever that began three days ago, two days after he returned from a two-week business trip to Thailand. He reports temperatures up to 102 F, a severe frontal headache with pain behind the eyes, muscle aches, joint aches, and marked fatigue, with mild nausea. He was bitten by mosquitoes frequently and did not use repellent regularly. He denies cough, shortness of breath, diarrhea, vomiting, neck stiffness, nosebleeds, and gum bleeding. He has no chronic medical conditions and takes no regular medications; he has taken acetaminophen 500 mg a few times for the fever with partial relief.

Vital signs in clinic: temperature 100.9 F, blood pressure 122/76, heart rate 88, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He appears ill but well hydrated. There is a faint blanching erythematous rash on the trunk. There is no jaundice and no lymphadenopathy, and the abdomen is soft without hepatosplenomegaly.

Test results today: dengue NS1 antigen positive, malaria blood smear negative, white blood cell count 3.1, platelets 98, hematocrit 44%.

Assessment is dengue fever without warning signs. Plan is supportive care with oral hydration and rest. Acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever and aches; he should avoid ibuprofen and aspirin because of the bleeding risk with low platelets. Repeat CBC with hematocrit in 48 hours in the clinic. Return precautions were reviewed: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, or drowsiness should prompt immediate emergency evaluation.

He was febrile at 100.9 F with a faint blanching rash on the trunk, and testing showed a positive dengue NS1 antigen, negative malaria smear, white blood cell count 3.1, and platelets 98. Management is supportive care with acetaminophen as needed, avoidance of ibuprofen and aspirin, a repeat CBC in 48 hours, and return precautions.

note:
Infectious disease inpatient follow-up dictation. This is a 51-year-old male with HIV seen on the ward for routine HIV follow-up while he is hospitalized for left lower leg cellulitis, hospital day 3. A professional Spanish interpreter was used for the entire visit, and I confirmed with teach-back that the patient understood. He has been on bictegravir, emtricitabine, tenofovir alafenamide one tablet daily for four years and at first told me he has never missed a dose. Correction, after further questions he says he missed one dose last week when he was brought to the emergency department. He denies fever, chills, nausea, diarrhea, headache, night sweats, cough, and weight loss. He says the leg is less painful and the redness is shrinking. No new rashes and no oral thrush. He denies tobacco and drug use and drinks alcohol rarely.

Vital signs this morning, temperature 98.4 F, blood pressure 126/78, heart rate 74, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam he is comfortable, no oral thrush, no lymphadenopathy, heart regular, lungs clear, abdomen soft. The left lower leg has erythema that has receded from the marked border, mild warmth, no fluctuance, and no drainage.

Data today: HIV viral load undetectable at less than 20 copies, CD4 count 540. Creatinine 0.9. Syphilis screen negative.

Assessment, HIV infection, virologically suppressed on antiretroviral therapy and immunologically stable. Left lower leg cellulitis improving on cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours.

Plan, continue bictegravir, emtricitabine, tenofovir alafenamide one tablet daily without changes. Switch cefazolin to oral cephalexin 500 mg four times daily to complete seven days total, with discharge expected tomorrow. Counseled on daily adherence using the interpreter, and a refill was provided. Offer the influenza vaccine before discharge. Repeat viral load and CD4 count in six months. Return to the HIV clinic in three months, and the clinic will schedule a professional interpreter for that visit.

He denied fever, chills, and other systemic symptoms, and the leg erythema is receding with no fluctuance or drainage. Viral load was undetectable and CD4 count was 540. The assessment was virologically suppressed HIV infection and improving cellulitis; antiretrovirals continue unchanged, cefazolin is switched to oral cephalexin, and viral load and CD4 count will be repeated in six months.

note:
Hospital day 2 for this 16-year-old female admitted with nine days of heavy vaginal bleeding and symptomatic anemia. She was hospitalized three weeks ago for similar bleeding and was discharged on norethindrone acetate, which she stopped after five days because of nausea. Overnight she had two further episodes of heavy flow, soaking about one pad every two hours at the worst, but over the past 12 hours the flow has slowed to about one pad every four hours. She reports lightheadedness when standing and fatigue. She denies abdominal pain, fever, syncope, chest pain, and easy bruising. She says she has never been sexually active. Menarche was at age 12 with irregular cycles since, and there is no family history of bleeding disorders.

Current medications are norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily, restarted on admission, ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily, and ondansetron 4 mg IV as needed for nausea. She received one unit of packed red blood cells yesterday for a hemoglobin of 7.4.

Vital signs this morning: temperature 98.6 F, blood pressure 108/64 sitting, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. She is pale but alert and conversational, mucous membranes are moist, and her heart is regular without a murmur. The abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Pelvic examination was deferred. Hemoglobin is 8.6 this morning, platelets 312, INR 1.1, ferritin 6, TSH 1.8, and urine hCG is negative. Pelvic ultrasound shows a normal-appearing uterus and ovaries without a mass. A von Willebrand panel was sent and is pending.

My impression is acute abnormal uterine bleeding, most consistent with anovulatory bleeding, with iron deficiency anemia; a bleeding disorder has not yet been excluded.

Plan: continue norethindrone acetate 5 mg three times daily until the bleeding stops, then decrease to 5 mg once daily. Change ondansetron to the oral route, 4 mg as needed, and take medications with food to limit nausea. Continue ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily. Repeat hemoglobin tomorrow morning. Follow up the von Willebrand panel and consult hematology. Plan discharge once bleeding is minimal and hemoglobin is stable, with adolescent gynecology follow-up in one week.

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. I have you down as a 44-year-old male with ulcerative colitis who came in because of some bleeding. What's been going on?
Patient: Hi, doctor. I'm really worried. About four days ago I started having loose stools, four or five times a day, and twice there was blood in my stool. Is this a flare? Is it going to get worse? Do I need to go to the hospital?
Doctor: Let's take it one step at a time. How many stools do you usually have?
Patient: One or two, formed. I've been in remission for about two years on my mesalamine. Could it have stopped working?
Doctor: What dose do you take?
Patient: 2.4 grams once a day. I haven't missed any doses, I promise. Why did this happen?
Doctor: Good question, we'll get to that. Any fever or weight loss?
Patient: No fever. I get some mild cramping before I go, but no severe pain, and no weight loss that I can tell. I'm not waking up at night to go either. Should I be worried about cancer? Or an infection?
Doctor: I understand why you're anxious, and I'll explain everything. Have you taken any other medicines, like pain pills or antibiotics?
Patient: Well, I took ibuprofen, 400 mg, a few times last week for my back. No antibiotics. Is the ibuprofen a problem?
Doctor: It can be. Ibuprofen and similar pain relievers can trigger flares in ulcerative colitis. Let me examine you. Blood pressure is 124/78, pulse 84, temperature 98.6, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Your abdomen is soft, with mild tenderness in the left lower area, no guarding, and normal bowel sounds. Your quick blood test here shows hemoglobin 14.1 and white count 7.9, both normal.
Patient: So I'm not bleeding a lot? What does that mean? Should I get a colonoscopy right now?
Doctor: Your hemoglobin is normal, so you haven't lost much blood, and a colonoscopy is not needed today; your GI doctor can decide later. My impression is a mild flare of ulcerative colitis, likely triggered by the ibuprofen, and there are no signs of severe disease. Here is the plan. Stop the ibuprofen completely. For your back, use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed. Increase your mesalamine to 4.8 grams once a day, and add mesalamine suppository, 1 gram at bedtime for two weeks. I'll send a stool test for C. diff and a fecal calprotectin to make sure it's not an infection.
Patient: How long until it gets better? What if it gets worse? Can I call you?
Doctor: Most people improve within one to two weeks. Go to the emergency department if you have more than six stools a day, heavy bleeding, fever, severe belly pain, or feel dizzy. Please see your GI doctor within two weeks.
Patient: Okay. Thank you for explaining. I feel a little better now.
summary: A 44-year-old male with ulcerative colitis in remission for about two years on mesalamine presented to urgent care anxious about four days of loose stools with blood on two occasions. He reported mild cramping and denied fever, severe pain, weight loss, and nighttime stools, and he had used ibuprofen a few times last week for back pain. Blood pressure was normal, the abdomen showed mild left lower tenderness without guarding, and hemoglobin and white count were normal. The impression was a mild flare of ulcerative colitis, likely triggered by ibuprofen. Ibuprofen was stopped, acetaminophen was given for back pain, oral mesalamine was increased with a mesalamine suppository added, and stool testing for C. diff and fecal calprotectin was sent.

soap.subjective: 44-year-old male with ulcerative colitis, in remission for about two years on mesalamine 2.4 grams once a day with no missed doses. Four days of loose stools four or five times a day with blood in the stool on two occasions. Mild cramping before stools. Denies fever, severe pain, weight loss, and waking at night to go. soap.objective: BP 124/78, pulse 84, temperature 98.6, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Abdomen soft with mild tenderness in the left lower area, no guarding, normal bowel sounds. Hemoglobin 14.1 and white count 7.9, both normal.

plan: Stop ibuprofen
Acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for back pain
Increase mesalamine to 4.8 grams once a day
Add mesalamine suppository 1 gram at bedtime for two weeks
Send a stool test for C. diff and a fecal calprotectin
Colonoscopy not needed today; GI doctor to decide later
Go to the emergency department for more than six stools a day, heavy bleeding, fever, severe belly pain, or dizziness
See the GI doctor within two weeks

Chief Complaint: Left forearm laceration.

HPI: 34-year-old male presents about one hour after cutting his left forearm on a broken drinking glass while washing dishes at home. Bleeding was controlled with direct pressure using a towel. He reports mild wound pain, 3 out of 10. He denies numbness, tingling, and weakness of the hand or fingers. Last tetanus vaccine was about 11 years ago. He was hospitalized three weeks ago for acute appendicitis and underwent a laparoscopic appendectomy, was discharged on hospital day 2, and has had no complications since. Home medication is acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for residual soreness. No known drug allergies.

ROS: Negative for fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, chest pain, and shortness of breath.

Physical Exam: Vitals: BP 134/82, HR 88, RR 16, Temp 98.4 F, SpO2 99% on room air. General: well-appearing, no acute distress. Left volar forearm: 4 cm linear laceration with clean edges extending into subcutaneous fat; no tendon exposed and no visible foreign body. Full active range of motion of the wrist and all fingers with 5/5 strength. Sensation intact in the median, ulnar, and radial distributions. Radial pulse 2+, capillary refill under 2 seconds. Abdomen: laparoscopic port sites are healing well, clean and nontender, no erythema or drainage.

ED Course / Results: X-ray of the left forearm shows no fracture and no radiopaque foreign body. Wound irrigation with 500 mL of normal saline was performed. Local anesthesia was achieved with 5 mL of 1% lidocaine. The laceration was closed with six simple interrupted 4-0 nylon sutures with good approximation and hemostasis. Tdap 0.5 mL IM was given.

Medical Decision Making: 34-year-old male with a simple forearm laceration without tendon, nerve, or vascular injury and no foreign body on imaging. His recent hospitalization and appendectomy do not change wound management, and the port sites show no sign of infection. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for this clean wound. Tdap was given because his last tetanus booster was more than 10 years ago.

Disposition: Discharged home in stable condition. Increase acetaminophen to 1000 mg every 6 hours as needed and start ibuprofen 400 mg every 6 hours as needed with food. Keep the wound clean and dry for 24 hours, then wash gently. Suture removal in 10 to 14 days with primary care. Return for redness, drainage, fever, numbness, or loss of finger movement. Keep the scheduled postoperative appointment.

Exam showed a 4 cm clean laceration with intact tendon function, sensation, and perfusion, and X-ray showed no fracture or foreign body. After irrigation and local anesthesia the wound was closed with six simple interrupted nylon sutures and Tdap was given. He was discharged on increased acetaminophen and newly started ibuprofen, with suture removal in 10 to 14 days and return precautions.

note:
Doctor: Hello, I'm the emergency physician. I have you down as a 61-year-old male, and I can see your lips are swollen. When did this start?
Patient: About an hour ago. We had shrimp pasta for dinner, and within half an hour my lips started tingling and swelling. Then my tongue felt thick and I got hives on my chest and arms. They're very itchy. A little later my throat started getting tight, so my wife drove me here.
Doctor: Any trouble breathing, wheezing, vomiting, or dizziness?
Patient: I can breathe okay, no trouble breathing, no wheezing, no vomiting. No dizziness and I haven't passed out.
Doctor: Have you eaten shrimp before without problems?
Patient: Yes, many times. This has never happened to me.
Doctor: Do you have any medical conditions, and what medicines do you take?
Patient: I have atrial fibrillation. I take apixaban 5 mg twice a day as a blood thinner. No known drug allergies and no new medicines lately.
Doctor: Thank you. Your blood pressure is 142/88, pulse 104, respiratory rate 20, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. You have swelling of the lips and tongue and hives on the chest and arms. Your voice is clear with no stridor, and your lungs are clear without wheezing.
Doctor: This is an allergic reaction with angioedema, most likely from the shrimp. Because your throat feels tight, I'm treating it urgently. I'm giving epinephrine 0.3 mg into your thigh muscle right now, plus diphenhydramine 50 mg and methylprednisolone 125 mg through the IV. Because you take apixaban, I'll hold firm pressure on the injection site for five minutes to limit bruising. I'm also getting an ECG, since epinephrine can speed up the heart, and I'll send a tryptase level and a basic metabolic panel.
Patient: Is it going to get worse? Will I be okay?
Doctor: Most people respond well. We'll watch you here for at least six hours.
Doctor: It's been about two hours and the swelling is going down. The ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 98 with no ischemic changes, and your creatinine is 1.1. After six hours of observation your throat is no longer tight and the hives are fading, so you can go home. Keep taking apixaban 5 mg twice a day as you do now. I'm prescribing prednisone 40 mg once a day for three days, and an epinephrine auto-injector to use in your thigh if the symptoms return, and then call emergency services. Avoid shrimp and other shellfish, and I'm referring you to an allergist. Come back right away for trouble breathing, throat tightness, or swelling that returns.
Patient: Thank you, doctor. That makes me feel better.
summary: A 61-year-old male on apixaban for atrial fibrillation presented to the emergency department with lip and tongue swelling, itchy hives, and a tight throat that began within half an hour of eating shrimp. He denied trouble breathing, wheezing, vomiting, dizziness, and syncope, and had no stridor on exam. Vital signs showed blood pressure 142/88, pulse 104, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The impression was an allergic reaction with angioedema, most likely from shrimp, and he received epinephrine, diphenhydramine, and methylprednisolone with firm pressure at the injection site because of apixaban. After six hours of observation he improved and was discharged on prednisone with an epinephrine auto-injector, shellfish avoidance, and an allergist referral.

Doctor: Hello, I have you down as an 85-year-old male who cut his arm. What happened?
Patient: I was opening boxes at work with a box cutter and it slipped. I work nights as a security guard at a warehouse, and my shifts change all the time, some nights, some weekends.
Doctor: Let me see. Does it hurt, and is it still bleeding?
Patient: It's my left forearm. There's some pain, but the bleeding stopped after I pressed a towel on it.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling in your fingers? Can you make a fist?
Patient: No numbness, no tingling, and I can move all my fingers.
Doctor: Do you take any blood thinners or other medicines?
Patient: No blood thinners. I have high blood pressure, and I take amlodipine 5 mg a day.
Doctor: When was your last tetanus shot?
Patient: I don't remember. Maybe fifteen years ago.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure is 138/80 and your pulse is 76. The cut is about five centimeters long on the left forearm, the edges are clean, I don't see any tendon, your grip is strong, and the feeling in your hand is normal. This is a laceration that needs stitches. I'll wash it out, numb it, and close it with stitches. Because your last tetanus shot was over ten years ago, I'll give you a tetanus booster too. Since your work schedule is irregular, I'll use stitches that dissolve so you don't need a separate visit to take them out. For pain you can take acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours if needed. Keep the dressing dry for two days.
Patient: Can I go back to work tomorrow night?
Doctor: Light duty with no heavy lifting for one week. Have your own doctor look at the wound any day that fits your shift, and come back sooner if it gets red, swollen, or starts draining, or if you get a fever.
Patient: That works. Thank you.
summary: An 85-year-old male who works irregular night shifts as a security guard cut his left forearm with a box cutter at work. He had some pain, the bleeding had stopped, and he denied numbness and tingling; he has high blood pressure treated with amlodipine and takes no blood thinners. Blood pressure was 138/80 and pulse 76, and the 5 cm laceration had clean edges with normal grip and sensation. It will be closed with dissolving stitches so no removal visit is needed, and a tetanus booster will be given because his last shot was over ten years ago. He was advised to use acetaminophen, do light duty for one week, and watch for infection.

Doctor: Hi, what brings you in today? I have you down as a 36-year-old female with back pain.
Patient: Yes. For about a week I've had low back pain that shoots down my right leg, from my buttock down the back of my thigh to my calf. It started after I lifted a heavy box while moving. My right foot has been tingling too.
Doctor: Any weakness in the leg, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, or fever?
Patient: No weakness, no numbness in the groin, no trouble with my bladder or bowels, and no fever.
Doctor: Good. Do you have help at home?
Patient: Not really. I live alone and my family is far away, so it's been hard to shop for groceries or even get to the pharmacy.
Doctor: I understand. Let me examine you. Blood pressure is 118/70 and pulse is 72. You're tender over the right lower back muscles. The straight leg raise on the right reproduces the pain down your leg at about 40 degrees. Strength is normal in both legs, reflexes are normal, and sensation is slightly decreased on the outside of the right calf.
Doctor: This is a right lumbar radiculopathy, probably from a herniated disc, and there are no red flags like weakness or bladder problems. Most people improve within six weeks without surgery. I'm starting naproxen 500 mg twice a day with food for 10 days. Stay gently active and avoid heavy lifting. I'm referring you to physical therapy, and if you're not better in six weeks, we'll get an MRI. Since you live alone, I'm asking our social worker to call you tomorrow about grocery delivery and rides to therapy.
Patient: Thank you. That would really help. What if my leg gets weak?
Doctor: Come back or go to the emergency department right away for leg weakness, numbness in the groin, or loss of bladder or bowel control. Follow up with orthopedics in two weeks.
summary: A 36-year-old female who lives alone with limited support presented to urgent care with one week of low back pain radiating down the right leg and right foot tingling after lifting a heavy box. She denied weakness, groin numbness, bladder or bowel trouble, and fever. Exam showed right lower back tenderness, a positive right straight leg raise at about 40 degrees, normal strength and reflexes, and slightly decreased sensation on the outside of the right calf. The impression was right lumbar radiculopathy, probably from a herniated disc, with no red flags. Naproxen, physical therapy, and a social worker call were arranged, with an MRI if not better in six weeks and orthopedics follow-up in two weeks.

Rheumatology outpatient dictation. This is a 57-year-old female with psoriatic arthritis and plaque psoriasis, here for follow-up of a flare. She tells me she has taken her adalimumab 40 mg, which is supposed to be every other week, only about once a month for the past four months because the copay went up and she cannot afford it. She continues methotrexate 15 mg once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily as prescribed. Over the last six weeks she has had swelling and pain in the right second and third fingers, morning stiffness lasting about 90 minutes, and a sausage-like swelling of the right third finger. Her scaly plaques on the elbows and scalp have also worsened. She is taking naproxen 500 mg twice daily with partial relief and lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension. She denies fever, eye redness, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and mouth ulcers.

Vital signs, blood pressure 146/88, heart rate 78, weight 172 pounds. On exam the right second and third proximal interphalangeal joints are swollen and tender, with dactylitis of the right third finger. Total of six tender and three swollen joints. There are scaly plaques on both elbows and the scalp covering about three percent of body surface area, and mild nail pitting. No uveitis, no knee effusion.

Labs today: CRP 2.4 mg/dL, elevated, ESR 34, ALT 26, creatinine 0.8, hemoglobin 12.9, white blood cell count 6.2. Hand x-rays show mild joint space narrowing at the right third proximal interphalangeal joint without erosions.

Assessment, psoriatic arthritis with an active flare, driven mainly by missed adalimumab doses because of cost. Blood pressure is elevated, likely aggravated by naproxen.

Plan, increase methotrexate to 20 mg once weekly and continue folic acid 1 mg daily. Stop naproxen because of the blood pressure; continue lisinopril 10 mg daily and have primary care recheck her blood pressure in two weeks. Refer to our social worker and pharmacy team to apply for the manufacturer copay assistance program, and restart adalimumab 40 mg every other week once it is approved. If assistance is denied, we will discuss a lower-cost biosimilar. Repeat CRP, CBC, and ALT in four weeks for methotrexate monitoring. Follow up in six weeks.
